rule: Every domain noun named or clearly implied by the feature description is accounted for in the produced data-model.md — modeled as an entity, or carried as an attribute or relationship of one. No named domain concept is silently absent.

No modeled entity is a single-value concept. Every entity in the document has its own lifecycle and carries more than one meaningful attribute beyond identity/audit fields; concepts holding exactly one value appear as attributes of another entity instead.
A concept that connects two entities appears as a documented relationship (or a join entity), never as a loose attribute on one side with no relationship entry.
Every entity carries a brownfield status marker drawn from exactly this set: [NEW], [EXTENDS EXISTING], [REUSES EXISTING], [RENAMED].
Any entity marked [RENAMED] states both the new name and the reason for the rename.
Every entity's attribute set includes id, createdAt, and updatedAt.
Where the document states or implies soft delete for an entity, that entity carries a deletedAt timestamp attribute marked not-required.

Every attribute type is a conceptual type, not a database-specific one. The document contains no SQL/DDL types (VARCHAR, INT, SERIAL, BIGINT, TEXT NOT NULL, NUMERIC, TIMESTAMPTZ), no CREATE TABLE, and no index/migration syntax.
source: SKILL.md:Conceptual Types / When NOT to Use

rule: Every entity has an Attributes table whose columns are Attribute, Type, Required, Default, Sensitivity, Description — and every row fills Type, Required, Sensitivity, and Description.
Every attribute row states an explicit required flag (Yes/No), never blank.
Enumerated attributes spell their value set inline in the type as Enum[value,value,...], not as a bare 'Enum' or 'String'.
Cross-entity reference attributes carry the type Reference(<EntityName>), naming the target entity.

Every attribute of every entity carries exactly one sensitivity classification, and that classification is one of the four words Public, Internal, Confidential, Restricted — no fifth level, no blank cell, no two levels on one attribute.
Highly sensitive data — credentials or password hashes, government identifiers (SSN/national id), payment card numbers, and health records — is classified Restricted, never Confidential or lower.
Standard PII — email address, phone number, postal address, personal name, date of birth — is classified Confidential (or Restricted), never Internal or Public.
PII is expressed through the sensitivity classification only. The document carries no parallel PII axis — no separate PII column, no 'PII: yes' tag, no PII marker alongside the classification.
source: SKILL.md:Classification Levels (PII mapping paragraph); DATA-SENSITIVITY.md:Validation Checklist

rule: Data intended for public sharing is classified Public, and internal operational data carrying no PII (internal ids, status codes, counters, timestamps) is classified Internal — not uniformly escalated to Confidential.
Where an attribute's sensitivity is genuinely ambiguous, it is classified up to Confidential rather than down to Internal or Public.
Every entity's Attributes table contains a Sensitivity column (the classification lives in the attribute table, not only in a separate list).

The handling-by-level defaults matrix (encryption at rest/in transit, audit logging, masking) appears exactly once in the whole document, placed under the sensitivity summary — never repeated per entity or per attribute.

Every attribute classified Confidential or Restricted has exactly one corresponding row in its own entity's Sensitivity Details table. No Confidential+ attribute is missing a row; no attribute has two rows.
source: SKILL.md:Annotating Sensitivity step 3; DATA-SENSITIVITY.md:Sensitivity Details Row Format

rule: The Sensitivity Details table columns are Attribute, Level, Retention, Access, Deviations, Compliance — in that order.
Sensitivity Details rows record only per-attribute specifics and deviations. Encryption, audit, and masking defaults already carried by the level matrix are not restated per attribute.
source: SKILL.md:Annotating Sensitivity step 3; DATA-SENSITIVITY.md:Sensitivity Annotation — Field Definitions

rule: Every Confidential+ attribute's row states a retention period AND what happens at expiry (delete, purge, anonymize) — a duration alone is incomplete.
source: DATA-SENSITIVITY.md:Sensitivity Annotation — Field Definitions / Validation Checklist

rule: Every Confidential+ attribute's row states access control in role terms — who may read, write, or delete it.
source: DATA-SENSITIVITY.md:Sensitivity Annotation — Field Definitions / Validation Checklist

rule: The Deviations cell reads em-dash when the attribute's handling is exactly its level default; any departure from the level default (weaker or stronger encryption, audit, or masking) is spelled out in that cell, never left silent.
source: DATA-SENSITIVITY.md:Sensitivity Details Row Format / Validation Checklist

rule: Where a Confidential+ attribute appears in logs or UIs, its attribute-specific masking format is named concretely (e.g. a masked example), not left to the level default.
source: DATA-SENSITIVITY.md:Sensitivity Annotation — Field Definitions / Validation Checklist

rule: The document opens with a Data Sensitivity Summary table with columns Entity, Attribute, Classification, Compliance, and that table lists every Confidential and Restricted attribute in the document — it is the artifact's coverage index.
source: SKILL.md:Annotating Sensitivity step 4; DATA-SENSITIVITY.md:Data Sensitivity Summary

rule: Where a regulation plainly applies to an attribute (GDPR for EU personal data, HIPAA for health data, PCI-DSS for card data, NIST 800-63 for credentials, SOC 2 for customer data), the compliance cell names the regulation, not a blank.

No per-attribute aspect table exists anywhere in the document — sensitivity handling is carried by rows in the Sensitivity Details table (plus at most a one-line footnote), never by a dedicated multi-row table per attribute.
Every relationship in the document states both its cardinality (1:1, 1:N, or N:M) and its delete behavior. A relationship missing either is a lost rule.
source: SKILL.md:Relationship Modeling / Quality Checklist; RELATIONSHIP-PATTERNS.md:Validation Checklist

rule: Every attribute typed Reference(...) has a matching documented relationship entry naming the same target entity.
Each relationship names where the foreign key lives (which entity holds the reference field, e.g. task.userId).
Delete behavior is drawn from the named set: Cascade, Set Null, Restrict, or No Action — not free-form prose such as 'handled by the app'.
Per-entity relationship tables carry the columns Relationship, Cardinality (or Type), Target, Delete Behavior, Description.
Every Many-to-Many (N:M) relationship is realized through a named join entity that is itself fully defined in the document with its own attributes table.
Each join entity carries a compound-unique constraint over its two foreign keys (the pair can be joined only once) plus whatever additional fields the relationship needs.
Each relationship makes direction explicit — which side is the one and which is the many (e.g. N:1 to User, or From/To rows) — not a bare 'related to'.
Any relationship where an entity references itself is explicitly marked as self-referential (tree or graph).
A text relationship diagram is present and every edge it draws corresponds to a relationship documented in a table (and vice versa) — the diagram matches the documentation.
Every entity carrying a status or state attribute has a documented state machine in the State Machines section.
source: SKILL.md:State Machine Modeling; STATE-MACHINES.md:When to Model State

rule: Each state machine has a States table with columns State, Description, Entry Condition, and state values written in backticks.
source: STATE-MACHINES.md:State Machine Format / State Documentation Components

rule: Each state machine has a Transitions table with columns From, To, Trigger, Guard, Side Effects.
source: STATE-MACHINES.md:State Machine Format / State Documentation Components

rule: The initial state is identifiable (marked as initial, or the only state whose entry condition is creation), and every state listed in the States table is reachable via at least one documented transition.
Terminal states — states with no outgoing transition — are identified as terminal where they exist.
Guards name the actor or condition permitting the transition (e.g. 'User is owner', 'Is admin', 'Has payment'), or read em-dash when unguarded — never left blank.
source: STATE-MACHINES.md:Guards and Side Effects / Validation Checklist

rule: Transitions that change other data list their side effects (timestamp set, notification sent, audit record written, related entity updated).
source: STATE-MACHINES.md:Guards and Side Effects / Validation Checklist

rule: Each state machine carries a diagram, and every arrow in the diagram corresponds to a row in its Transitions table.
The State Machines section is omitted entirely when the model has no stateful entity — it never appears as an empty heading or a 'None / N/A' placeholder.

Transitions are enumerated as a closed set, so that any From-To pair absent from the table reads as forbidden; the document does not leave transition legality open-ended with phrases like 'and other transitions as needed'.
Uniqueness constraints are documented for every attribute that must be unique, and scoped uniqueness is written with its scope (e.g. Unique(projectId)) rather than as bare 'Unique'.
source: VALIDATION-RULES.md:Validation Column Patterns / Compound Unique Constraints

rule: Format-typed attributes (email, url, phone, slug, uuid, iso8601 dates) carry an explicit format or pattern validation.
Bounded values carry their bounds: numeric range/min/max for quantities, amounts and counts; length bounds for free-text fields.
Cross-field business rules are documented with the fields involved, the condition, and the error message (e.g. endDate >= startDate).
Foreign key constraints are listed with their on-delete behavior, consistent with the delete behavior stated on the corresponding relationship.
Validation that applies only in certain states is recorded as conditional validation naming the state (e.g. reviewerId required when status is submitted).
Entity-level constraints appear in a table with columns Name, Type, Fields, Rule, using the uk_ / chk_ / fk_ naming convention for constraint names.
The document title is 'Data Model: <feature identifier>' as a single level-1 heading.
A one-line purpose blockquote sits directly under the title, naming what the document carries (entity definitions with relationships, sensitivity annotations, state machines).
Sections appear in this order: Data Sensitivity Summary (with handling defaults), Entity Summary, per-entity sections, Relationships, State Machines, Validation Rules.
An Entity Summary table is present with columns Entity, Attributes, Relationships, Status, and it lists every entity defined in the document.

Each entity gets its own section headed 'Entity: <Name> [STATUS]', and the entity names used in that heading match the names used in the Entity Summary, the Data Sensitivity Summary, and the relationship tables — identical spelling throughout.
An entity marked [EXTENDS EXISTING] separates new attributes from a distinct 'Existing Attributes (Not Modified)' table rather than mixing them into one list.
Each entity section carries a traceability line citing the upstream requirement or story identifiers it serves.
Upstream requirements are cited by identifier, never re-quoted at length — a traceability citation is the ID link, not a restatement of the requirement text.
source: templates/artifact-format.md:Shared rules 1 (envelope, cited by SKILL.md:data-model.md Structure)

rule: Enumerable content (attributes, relationships, states, transitions, constraints) is carried in tables; prose is reserved for judgment and rationale.
Sections with nothing to say are omitted, never written as 'None' or 'N/A' scaffolding.

The artifact does not restate method or doctrine — no explanation of the classification taxonomy, no decision tree, no modeling-technique lecture. The single exception is the handling-by-level defaults matrix, which the self-containment floor requires once.
No anemic entity: no entity is defined with only an id (plus audit fields) and no attributes describing its purpose.
No orphan entity: every entity participates in at least one documented relationship, or is explicitly stated to be standalone.
The document contains no API contract content — no HTTP endpoints, methods, status codes, OpenAPI/Swagger YAML, or request/response schema definitions.
The document contains no database-implementation content — no migration scripts, index definitions, storage engines, partitioning, or physical schema.
The document contains no technology or architecture decision content — no framework, datastore-product, or library choice, no ADR-style alternatives evaluation.
